title: Help: ingredients and workflow
text: This is a small, static Quarto website with interactive mathematics running in the reader’s browser. You can edit it locally in VS Code or work on the source through a GitHub-connected assistant. Both routes use the same source files and build process.

title: Help: ingredients and workflow
text:
Who does what, and when?
Here, GH-adapter means the GitHub connection used by an assistant to read repository files and submit changes. It is an authoring connection, not a component loaded by this website. The website also works without an assistant.





flowchart TD
  H["Human: request or edit"] --> A["Assistant + GH-adapter"]
  H --> V["VS Code + local Git"]
  A --> R["Branch and pull request"]
  V --> R
  R --> C["Actions: check build"]
  C --> M["Human: review and merge"]
  M --> B["Actions: setup and render main"]
  B --> P["Publish gh-pages"]
  P --> U["Browser: applets and Python"]













Stage
Responsibility




Request
The human specifies the content, expected behavior, and scope.


Edit
A human in VS Code or an assistant through the adapter updates .qmd, .md, .yml, or supporting files. The adapter transfers repository changes; it does not run the website.


Check
A pull request triggers a render check. Local preview and browser testing check layout, interactions, and mathematical behavior. A successful render alone does not prove the applets work.


Review
The human reviews the diff and merges the pull request. This is the recommended workflow for subsequent changes.


Publish
A push to main runs scripts/setup.py, renders the website, and writes the output to gh-pages.


Read
GitHub Pages serves static files. The browser loads the interactive libraries and executes the examples. No Python application server is needed.

title: Help: ingredients and workflow
section: Set up locally in VS Code
text:
Set up locally in VS Code
Install Git, Python 3.12, Quarto CLI, and VS Code. The Quarto VS Code extension is useful, but does not replace the Quarto CLI. Open the repository folder, not just a file.
git clone https://github.com/aacchhee/ctm-demo.git
cd ctm-demo
python -m venv .venv
Activate the environment:

macOS / LinuxWindows PowerShell


source .venv/bin/activate
If your system uses python3, use it instead of python when creating the environment.


.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
If script activation is unavailable, call .venv\Scripts\python.exe directly in the Python commands below. You can use py -3.12 to create the environment.



Then install the build dependencies and extensions:
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
python scripts/setup.py
quarto preview
Open the localhost URL printed by Quarto. Do not open generated HTML directly with file://: the browser runtime uses workers and network requests. In VS Code, accept the recommended Quarto and Python extensions, and select .venv as the Python interpreter. Terminal → Run Task → Preview website starts the preview; Build website renders to _site/.
The Python setup script installs Quarto extensions listed in quarto-extensions.yml. It requires Git and Quarto on PATH. The same command runs locally and in GitHub Actions; it does not install Python or Quarto itself. Re-running it updates extensions to their configured refs. Those refs currently follow upstream branches, so later setup runs can obtain newer extension code.

title: Help: ingredients and workflow
text:
Publish with GitHub Pages
After the first successful build has created gh-pages, the repository owner sets Settings → Pages → Build and deployment → Source: Deploy from a branch, then selects gh-pages / (root) and saves. This is a one-time repository setting; committing the workflow does not configure it automatically.
Subsequent pushes to main build and publish automatically. Pull requests build without publishing. The workflow can also be started from Actions → Build and publish → Run workflow. GitHub Actions must be enabled, and repository policy must permit the workflow’s contents: write permission.
The intended website address is https://aacchhee.github.io/ctm-demo/. When copying this repository, change website.site-url in _quarto.yml and these repository links to match the new owner and name.

Site title, sidebar, rendered pages, filters, and English language.

Extension repositories, refs, and installation paths.

Shared extension installer for local development and CI.


styles.css, _includes/site/
Small presentation and navigation helpers.



For an additional page, create a .qmd file and add it to both project.render and website.sidebar.contents in _quarto.yml. Use relative page links so navigation works both on localhost and under the GitHub Pages repository path. Do not edit _site/, _extensions/, or .private-extensions/: they are generated or downloaded, ignored by Git, and may be replaced.

A tiny Python exercise to reuse
This is a source example, not an extra exercise on the demo page. Paste it into pages/experiments.qmd to try the installed Python exercise extension:
```{py-exercise}
#| label: add-two-numbers
#| caption: Implement addition
def add(a, b):
    pass

## TESTS ##
assert add(1, 2) == 3, "Check addition of positive numbers."
assert add(-1, 1) == 0, "Check addition with a negative number."
```
Use unique labels when copying cells. Tests are hidden from the normal exercise view, but remain downloadable in a static site; these exercises provide practice feedback rather than secure examination grading.

title: Help: ingredients and workflow
text:
Using and troubleshooting the demo

Python is still loading: the first visit downloads the browser runtime and packages. Wait for the ready indicator. Internet access to the upstream CDNs is needed; this is not a self-contained offline bundle.
A name such as np or power_iteration is missing: let the automatic setup cells finish, or rerun the relevant definition before running the dependent cell. Cells on the demo page share Python state; a reload starts a new session.
Quarto cannot find a filter: run python scripts/setup.py from your checkout and read the first error. Confirm that Git and Quarto are installed and that the configured extension repositories and refs are reachable.
The local build succeeds but the public page is old: check the latest Actions run and the Pages branch setting. Browser refresh may also be needed.
Feedback asks for provider settings: deterministic calculations and answer checking do not need an AI API key. Where the extension offers AI feedback, its copy-prompt mode lets you use an external assistant manually. Direct API feedback uses your configured provider and may incur that provider’s charges. Keep keys out of source files and commits.

Before publishing an edit, try the applet’s presets and reset, run the Python cells, and submit both correct and incorrect mathematical answers. Check a narrow browser window as well as a desktop layout.

title: Interactive mathematics
text:
Explore a direction, run Python in your browser, and check your mathematics. Use the tabs to move between the examples and problems.


Explore


Go deeper




Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

1 A direction emerges2 The power method3 Problems



Which direction remains?
We repeatedly apply the transformation \(T(x)=Ax\), represented in the standard basis by
\[A=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}.\]
Do sequences starting from different vectors approach the same line? Each click applies the transformation once, then sets the vector’s length to one. This lets us follow its direction without growing vectors leaving the picture.

Choose (1, 0). Predict which line the blue vector will approach. Click One step five times. Do the coordinates become closer?
Choose (−1, 0) and repeat. Is it the same line? The same orientation?
Choose (1, 1), then (1, −1). Take three steps from each starting vector. Does the direction change? Write down one observation for each.
Try (0, 1) and (1, −0.9). The latter is close to the special direction \((1,-1)^T\). Then drag the orange ring to choose your own starting vector.

The presets specify directions. To normalize a vector means to divide it by its length, giving a unit vector. The orange vector shows \(x_0\); the blue vector shows the normalized iterate \(x_k\). Each click computes \(Ax\) and divides the whole vector by its length. We do not normalize individual coordinates. The formula beside the blue endpoint identifies the iterate. You can drag the orange ring even when it surrounds the blue endpoint.



What did you notice?
For many starting vectors, the normalized iterates approach the same line, but their limiting vectors may point in opposite directions. Starting along \((1,1)^T\) or \((1,-1)^T\) leaves the direction unchanged.
Combine multiplication and normalization into one update rule:
\[F(x)=\frac{Ax}{\lVert Ax\rVert_2},\qquad x_{k+1}=F(x_k).\]
Here \(\lVert x\rVert_2\) is the usual vector length and \(k\) counts the steps. The rule is defined when \(Ax\ne0\).
Do you recognize this form from an iteration you already know? We put a value into a rule and use the result as the next value. What changes when the value is a vector? Which equation must hold if the next step is to return exactly the same vector?
After \(k\) steps,
\[x_k=\frac{A^kx_0}{\lVert A^kx_0\rVert_2}.\]
We set \(A^0=I\), the identity transformation. The starting vector in the figure has length one.
Discuss: Why can we discard length information and still see which direction dominates? What distinguishes the two special starting directions?


Go deeper: scaling without turning

Starting from \((1,0)^T\), the first step is
\[Ax_0=\begin{bmatrix}2\\1\end{bmatrix},\quad
\lVert Ax_0\rVert_2=\sqrt5,\quad
x_1=\frac1{\sqrt5}\begin{bmatrix}2\\1\end{bmatrix}.\]
Check: Multiply \((1,1)^T\) and \((1,-1)^T\) by \(A\). Do they turn, or are they just multiplied by a number?
For \(x=(a,b)^T\),
\[Ax=\begin{bmatrix}2a+b\\a+2b\end{bmatrix},\qquad
\lVert Ax\rVert_2=\sqrt{(2a+b)^2+(a+2b)^2}.\]
Dividing both coordinates by the same positive number preserves their ratio and the vector’s orientation. Only its length changes.
At the next step, the previous normalization cancels:
\[x_2=\frac{(5,4)^T/\sqrt5}{\sqrt{41}/\sqrt5}
=\frac{(5,4)^T}{\sqrt{41}}
=\frac{A^2x_0}{\lVert A^2x_0\rVert_2}.\]
This happens at every step, explaining the formula in the figure. We take small, normalized steps; we do not need to calculate \(A^k\) explicitly. The denominators must be nonzero.
Without normalization, the first vectors are \((1,0)^T,(2,1)^T,(5,4)^T,(14,13)^T\). The coordinate difference remains one, but becomes small relative to the vector’s size. The direction approaches the line whose two coordinates are equal.
The preset \((1,-1)\) uses \(x_0=(1,-1)^T/\sqrt2\). Here \(Ax_0=x_0\) from the start: this direction is an exception. In fact, the two special lines are eigenvector directions, with eigenvalues 3 and 1.





What determines the speed?
How quickly does the contribution along the eigenvector with the largest eigenvalue take over? Compare
\[A_\mu=Q\operatorname{diag}(3,\mu)Q^T,\qquad
Q=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{bmatrix}\]
for \(\mu=1\) and \(\mu=2.9\). The columns \(q_1,q_2\) of \(Q\) are orthonormal eigenvectors. Both sequences start at \(x_0=(1,0)^T\).
Write each iterate as \(x_k=b_1(k)+b_2(k)\), where \(b_i(k)=(q_i^Tx_k)q_i\). Compare the shares of their lengths:
\[a_i(k)=\frac{\lVert b_i(k)\rVert_2}
{\lVert b_1(k)\rVert_2+\lVert b_2(k)\rVert_2},\qquad i=1,2.\]

Blue: \(a_1(k)\). Orange: \(a_2(k)\).
Solid: \(\mu=1\). Dashed: \(\mu=2.9\).


Predict which pair of curves approaches 1 and 0 faster.
Run the cell. Compare the orange curves after ten steps.
How many steps does each orange curve need to fall below 0.1? What does this tell you about nearly equal eigenvalues?


Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
For \(\mu=1\), the blue share quickly approaches 1. For \(\mu=2.9\), the shares change slowly: the two contributions grow by almost the same factor at each step. The eigenvalue ratio \(\mu/3\) determines the speed.


Go deeper: connect the curves to the eigenvalues

The starting vector has equal coordinates along \(q_1\) and \(q_2\). After \(k\) multiplications, the ratio of contribution lengths is
\[r_k=\frac{\lVert b_2(k)\rVert_2}{\lVert b_1(k)\rVert_2}
=\left(\frac{|\mu|}{3}\right)^k.\]
The ratio \(r_k\) and share \(a_2(k)\) are different quantities:
\[a_1(k)=\frac1{1+r_k},\qquad a_2(k)=\frac{r_k}{1+r_k}.\]
Both shares start at \(1/2\). After ten steps, the orange share is approximately \(0.0000169\) for \(\mu=1\) and \(0.416\) for \(\mu=2.9\).
\[a_2(k)<0.1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad r_k<\frac19.\]
This requires 3 steps for \(\mu=1\) and 65 for \(\mu=2.9\). Check these counts using the expression for \(r_k\).
The exact recurrence \(r_{k+1}=(|\mu|/3)r_k\) resembles the local error model for a scalar fixed-point iteration: a factor close to one gives slow convergence. The code computes coordinates from iterated vectors, so rounding can affect very small contributions. A linear vertical axis does not reveal such tiny errors clearly.



Write down the algorithm
This is the power method:
Choose x ≠ 0 and divide it by its length.
Repeat, with a maximum number of steps:
    y = A x
    If y = 0: stop; normalization is impossible.
    x = y / ‖y‖₂
    Find a number ρ describing the scaling along x.
    Check how closely A x ≈ ρ x.
One step is multiplication followed by normalization:
\[y_k=Ax_k,\qquad x_{k+1}=\frac{y_k}{\lVert y_k\rVert_2}.\]


The power method as a fixed-point iteration
The update from 1 has the form \(x_{k+1}=F(x_k)\), where \(F(x)=Ax/\lVert Ax\rVert_2\). The power method is a fixed-point iteration. A fixed point \(x_*\) satisfies \(F(x_*)=x_*\). Normalization makes \(F\) nonlinear, even though \(x\mapsto Ax\) is linear.
If \(F(x_*)=x_*\), then
\[Ax_*=\lVert Ax_*\rVert_2\,x_*.\]
Thus a fixed point is a unit eigenvector for a positive eigenvalue; conversely, every such eigenvector is a fixed point. This does not mean every starting vector converges to it. The eigenvalues and the contributions present in the starting vector determine the outcome.
For a unit eigenvector \(v\) with a negative eigenvalue, \(F(v)=-v\) and \(F(-v)=v\). The iteration alternates between two vectors on one line. The line remains unchanged, but the vector is not a fixed point.


From projection to the Rayleigh quotient
The power method first finds a candidate direction \(x\). Which scalar \(t\) makes \(tx\) the best approximation to \(Ax\)? We want the orthogonal projection of \(Ax\) onto \(\operatorname{span}\{x\}\).
For \(x\ne0\), the projection of \(b\) onto that line is \(\frac{x^Tb}{x^Tx}x\). The inner product \(x^Tb=\sum_i x_i b_i\) gives the numerator; \(x^Tx=\lVert x\rVert_2^2\) corrects for the length of \(x\). Setting \(b=Ax\) gives
\[\rho(x)=\frac{x^TAx}{x^Tx},\qquad r=Ax-\rho(x)x,\qquad x^Tr=0.\]
The Rayleigh quotient \(\rho\) minimizes \(\lVert Ax-tx\rVert_2\) over all real \(t\). The eigenresidual \(r\) is the part of \(Ax\) perpendicular to \(x\) that cannot be described as scaling \(x\).
For \(x=(1,0)^T\) and the matrix in 1, \(Ax=(2,1)^T\). Its projection is \(2x\), so \(\rho=2\) and \(r=(0,1)^T\): \(x\) is not an eigenvector. For \(x=(1,1)^T/\sqrt2\), we get \(\rho=3\) and \(r=0\).
The eigenresidual tests \(Ax=\rho x\), whereas the fixed-point residual \(F(x)-x\) tests a different equation. For a unit eigenvector with a negative eigenvalue, the eigenresidual is zero but \(F(v)-v=-2v\).
What does a small residual tell us? The eigenvector equation is nearly satisfied. It does not prove that the eigenvalue is dominant: the direction with eigenvalue 1 also gives zero residual. For a general matrix it does not, by itself, guarantee proximity to a particular exact eigenvector.


Go deeper: why this quotient?

Orthogonality of the residual gives
\[x^T(Ax-\rho x)=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x^TAx-\rho x^Tx=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \rho=\frac{x^TAx}{x^Tx}.\]
For a unit vector, \(\rho=x^TAx\). A residual is a vector; its norm is a number. The code below records the quotient and the residual norm.
Calculate by hand: Use \(x=(2,1)^T/\sqrt5\), the first normalized step from 1. Calculate \(Ax\), \(\rho\), and \(r\), then compare with
\[Ax=\frac1{\sqrt5}\begin{bmatrix}5\\4\end{bmatrix},\qquad
\rho=\frac{14}{5},\qquad
r=\frac1{5\sqrt5}\begin{bmatrix}-3\\6\end{bmatrix},\qquad
\lVert r\rVert_2=\frac35.\]
The residual norm has decreased from 1 to \(3/5\) after one step.



Go deeper: implementation of the power method

The definition runs automatically. Follow the pseudocode: normalization, Rayleigh quotient, residual, and a maximum number of steps.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
y is \(Ax\), rho is \(x^TAx\), and residual is \(\lVert Ax-\rho x\rVert_2\). We record these before the next update, so the final row of history corresponds to the returned vector.
scale is the Frobenius norm \(\lVert A\rVert_F\), the square root of the sum of the squared matrix entries. For \(A\ne0\), the stopping test is \(\lVert r\rVert_2/\lVert A\rVert_F\le\text{tol}\). Scaling \(A\) by a common nonzero factor scales numerator and denominator equally. max_steps bounds experiments that do not converge.
If \(Ax=0\), \(x\) is already an eigenvector for zero, but the next normalization is impossible. The status message explains this case.


Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Read the status together with \(\rho\) and the residual. The tolerance controls the relative residual; it is not an absolute error bound for the eigenvalue.
